problem: relation has no index on dst. Its only index is the primary key (src, rel, dst), which cannot be searched by dst alone. relation.dst REFERENCES entity(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, so deleting each entity makes PostgreSQL find the relations that point at it with WHERE dst = <id>, and with no index that is a sequential scan of the 220 million-row relation table. The nightly purge deletes about 300,000 entities, so that is on the order of 300,000 scans (the src side is covered by the primary key; the dst side is the cost). This is why the purge overruns into the 03:00 crawl window.
fix: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY relation_by_dst ON relation (dst); (add it to schema.sql too). Expect a few GB and slightly slower relation writes. Do not index entity.kind_id: entity_kind rows are never updated or deleted, so no referential check ever needs it.

problem: One DELETE removes about 300,000 entities plus every relation pointing to or from them (probably over a million rows) in a single transaction. It holds row locks on all of them until the end, and crawl writers that upsert relations to those entities wait on the locks (the foreign key check needs a lock on the entity row). It also creates a huge burst of dead tuples and WAL, and if it is cancelled at 02:59 everything rolls back and the next night starts even further behind.
fix: Delete in batches that commit separately, e.g. repeat until 0 rows: DELETE FROM entity WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM entity WHERE last_seen < now() - interval '90 days' ORDER BY last_seen LIMIT 5000 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED); with a short pause between batches, stopping before 03:00 and resuming the next night.

problem: Index (last_seen) is right for the purge's range predicate and does not need to change. Note, however, that nothing in this repo (queries/upsert_relation.sql only sets relation.seen) updates entity.last_seen, so if the crawl writers do not refresh it elsewhere, live entities will be purged after 90 days.
fix: Confirm the crawl updates entity.last_seen whenever it sees an entity; otherwise add that to the writers before relying on the purge.

problem: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET seen = excluded.seen rewrites the row on every re-crawl of an existing relation, producing a new tuple version and dead tuple each time. On 220 million relations that is steady bloat and autovacuum load, and it adds to what the purge has to compete with. It also takes row locks that queue behind the purge's locks.
fix: Only update when the value is meaningfully older, e.g. DO UPDATE SET seen = excluded.seen WHERE relation.seen < excluded.seen - interval '1 day', and consider fillfactor 90 on relation so updates can stay on the same page (HOT).

problem: No vacuum or autovacuum settings for the tables hit hardest by the nightly deletes. Default autovacuum thresholds scale with table size, so on 220 million rows dead tuples build up for a long time between runs.
fix: Set per-table storage parameters, for example ALTER TABLE relation SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01); same for entity, and run a manual VACUUM after the purge window if needed.

problem: The primary key (src, rel, dst) serves WHERE r.src = $1 and the join to entity uses the primary key, but ORDER BY r.rel, e.label LIMIT 200 has to fetch and sort every neighbour of the source before it can return 200 rows (the sort is on e.label, which is not in any index). A hub entity with millions of relations makes that query slow. There is also no tie-breaker for equal rel and label.
fix: Order by r.rel, r.dst (served by the primary key) and keyset-paginate, or cap the fan-out before the join; add , e.id as the final sort key if the order must be stable.

problem: Counts across all 60 million entities every week, a full scan joined to a 12-row table. Acceptable for a weekly dashboard but it gets slower as the table grows and competes for IO.
fix: Group by e.kind_id and join entity_kind afterwards, or keep the counts in a small summary table refreshed after the purge. No index is needed for this.

problem: The db service has no data volume, so the database is lost whenever the container is recreated, and the postgres image only runs schema.sql on an empty data directory, so schema changes such as the missing index are never applied to an existing database. The password is hard-coded as dev-only.
fix: Add a named volume for /var/lib/postgresql/data, apply schema changes with migrations (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY run by hand on the live database), and keep the compose file explicitly dev only.
